items.justification: Physical interface exposure versus provenance documentation for public training data.
Credential change mechanism versus disclosure of data handling.
Both convey residual risk to stakeholders, A by recording unmet provisions and B by escalating unresolved threats down the supply chain.
Cryptographic protection in transit versus sharing test findings with operators.
Prohibiting hard-coded credentials and evaluating access-control frameworks are separate objectives that together determine whether credentials can be abused.
Cryptographic communication versus resilience to adversarial AI attack.
Installation usability versus action logging.
Input validation versus least-privilege permissions between systems.
Key lifecycle management versus model performance monitoring.
Both govern secure handling of sensitive assets across their lifecycle, including disposal; A for critical security parameters, B for training data and models on transfer.
Secure boot verification versus design and maintenance audit trail.
Update notification preferences versus incident support for end-users.
Both limit exposure of sensitive internals but by different means: protected storage versus evaluating outputs for leakage.
Confidentiality of parameters in transit versus internal involvement of Data Custodians.
Both require continuous monitoring and review for security weaknesses; A is vulnerability-focused with a duty to rectify, B is infrastructure risk review against risk appetite.
Key management processes versus audit logging of model configuration.
Documenting sensing capabilities versus patch provision.
Credential change mechanism versus pre-build risk assessment.
Deletion of personal data from services versus risk from superfluous model capability.
Physical attack surface versus technical measures enabling human oversight.
Verifying update authenticity and vetting the external provider are distinct objectives that together establish trust in what is received.
Authentication cryptography versus staff threat awareness.
Both reduce risk by removing capability that is not needed, A for exposed physical interfaces and B for superfluous model functionality.
Both mandate secure processes around how software is built and sourced; A names development practice, B names the supply chain.
Communication cryptography versus threat modelling on configuration change.
Update mechanism versus inter-system permissions.
Data deletion instructions versus external component due diligence.
Key management versus mitigating controls for poorly documented components.
Runtime verification of update integrity and design-time verification that specified controls were built in address different points in the assurance chain.
Outage resilience versus threat analysis and risk management.
Both aim at security being correctly built into the delivered software, A through development process and B through verification of specified controls.
Both require a vulnerability disclosure policy to be published and accessible; the differences are elaboration of the same obligation rather than of scope.
Authentication cryptography versus component due diligence.
Physical attack surface versus action logging.
Telemetry anomaly examination versus technical measures for human oversight.
Timely vulnerability remediation versus threat modelling on configuration change.
Both protect an exposed interface through access control against abuse; A covers debug interfaces, B covers externally offered APIs with rate limiting.
Both require documentation to be recorded and made available so downstream stakeholders can assess the security posture.
Update notification preferences versus threat modelling on configuration change.
Automatic update activation at initialization versus provision of usage guidance.
